Hazards_Annotation: Wind is the primary hazard throughout the event.

Time_Annotation: April 19, 1996– A series of tornadoes occurred: two brief F0 tornadoes in Coles County, F0 and F1 tornadoes in Edgar County, a brief F0 near Winchester, a strong F2 in Mason County, an F3 in Henry County injuring 4 people, plus additional tornadoes in Decatur, Salem, and Urbana with a total damage of up to $9 million.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Key areas include Coles, Edgar, Mason, Henry counties, and the cities of Decatur, Salem, and Urbana.
Main_Event_Annotation: The mixed ratings from F0 to F3 indicate a multi-faceted tornado outbreak.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind is the destructive agent in these tornado events.

Time_Annotation: April 15, 1998– A brief F0 tornado touched down north of Hoopole and west of Viola; another F0 in Red Bud caused no damage; additional F0 tornadoes occurred south of Marissa and in Washington County, with a tornado also videotaped near Coulterville.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The description includes locations such as Hoopole, Viola, Red Bud, Marissa, Washington County, Monroe, and St. Clair County.
Main_Event_Annotation: Various F0 and brief F1 tornadoes confirm the event as a tornado occurrence.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind from these brief tornadoes is the main hazard.

Time_Annotation: May 5, 1999– A brief F1 tornado touched down east of Kell, destroying a mobile home and injuring 4 occupants.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is described relative to the area east of Kell.
Main_Event_Annotation: The F1 rating identifies it as a tornado.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind is the usual hazard associated with an F1 tornado.

Event_Names: 2002 Tornado in St. Clair County, Kenner, Galatia, and Dongola Region
Time_Annotation: April 27, 2002– A brief F1 tornado touched down in St. Clair County and Kenner; an F2 tornado tracked through Galatia; a long-tracked intense tornado moved across Union and Johnson counties in Dongola, with additional F2 in Ganntown and an F3 in Pope County.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Locations include St. Clair, Kenner, Galatia, Union, Johnson, Dongola, Ganntown, and Pope County.
Main_Event_Annotation: Multiple tornado intensities (F1, F2, F3) confirm the event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage from the tornadoes is the primary hazard.

Event_Names: 2003 Tornado in Kentucky and Massac County
Time_Annotation: May 4, 2003– An F1 tornado touched down in Kentucky before crossing into Massac County, downing power lines and damaging trailers; twin tornadoes in Pope County produced F1-leveled tree damage before briefly crossing into Kentucky.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Affected areas are Kentucky, Massac County, and Pope County.
Main_Event_Annotation: F1 tornado events characterize this occurrence.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind hazards are associated with these F1 tornadoes.

Event_Names: 2003 Tornado in Monroe, Pulaski, Massac, and Alexander Counties
Time_Annotation: May 6, 2003– Multiple tornadoes were reported: an F1 tornado in Monroe County, an F1 east of Red Bud, brief F0 tornadoes in Walsh and near Miller City, a violent F4 tornado tracked 33 miles across Pulaski, Massac and Pope counties, an F0 in Cypress, an F2 in Alexander County crossing into Missouri, and additional brief F0 events in Johnson and Massac counties, with an F2 near Metropolis.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The description covers a broad region including Monroe, Red Bud, Walsh, Miller City, Pulaski, Massac, Pope, Cypress, Alexander, Johnson counties, and near Metropolis.
Main_Event_Annotation: The mix of F1, violent F4, F0, and F2 tornadoes indicates a complex tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the primary hazard across the multiple tornado reports.

Time_Annotation: May 8, 2003– A brief F0 tornado touched down west of Staunton and another F0 tornado touched down south of Oskaloosa.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event mentions locations near Staunton and Oskaloosa.
Main_Event_Annotation: The F0 ratings designate these as tornado events, albeit minor.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind, though less intense, is the hazard in these events.

Time_Annotation: May 9, 2003– A tornado inflicted F0-leveled damage to multiple homes and blew over a semi-truck in Sangamon County.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is noted in Sangamon County.
Main_Event_Annotation: This is identified as a tornado event based on damage description.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind, even at F0 intensity, is the hazard.

Time_Annotation: July 13, 2004– A violent F4 tornado moved west of Roanoke, injuring 3 and completely destroying a parts supplier factory for Caterpillar Inc.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event is associated with the area west of Roanoke.
Main_Event_Annotation: The F4 intensity confirms a major tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind is the destructive agent in this high-intensity tornado.

Event_Names: 2013 Tornado in Washington and Tazewell County
Time_Annotation: November 17, 2013– An unusually powerful EF4 tornado moved through Washington and several farmsteads in rural central Illinois, in Tazewell County, killing 3 and injuring 125.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The tornado affected areas in Washington and Tazewell County.
Main_Event_Annotation: An EF4 rating confirms this as a severe tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: The hazard is the extreme wind speeds associated with an EF4 tornado.

Event_Names: 2015 Tornado in Ogle County (Rochelle and Fairdale)
Time_Annotation: April 9, 2015– A violent EF4 tornado moved through Ogle County, directly impacting the communities of Rochelle and Fairdale, killing 2 and injuring 22; it was the strongest tornado in northern Illinois in 25 years.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event highlights Ogle County, with specific mention of Rochelle and Fairdale.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF4 classification confirms it as a major tornado.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the primary hazard in an EF4 tornado.

Time_Annotation: June 20, 2021– An EF3 tornado struck the Chicago suburbs of Naperville and Woodridge, damaging hundreds of structures, downing thousands of trees, and injuring 11 people; additionally, two EF0 tornadoes were reported near Romeoville and Addison.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The affected areas include Naperville, Woodridge, Romeoville, and Addison.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF3 classification and additional EF0 events confirm this as a tornado outbreak.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the primary hazard associated with these tornadoes.

Time_Annotation: March 31 – April 31, 2023– An EF1 tornado struck the Apollo Theatre in Belvidere, causing the collapse of the structure onto a concert with 260 people, injuring 40 and killing 1; an accompanying EF3 tornado produced damage in Illinois before crossing into Indiana.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event primarily affected Belvidere and later impacted areas in Indiana.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF1 and EF3 ratings confirm this tornado event.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind, causing structural collapse and widespread damage, is the hazard.

Event_Names: 2023 Tornado near Marcelline, Jackson, and Jasper Counties
Time_Annotation: August 5, 2023– A relatively brief EF2 tornado tracked 2.87 miles near Marcelline, damaging numerous homes and downing power lines; additionally, an EF0 tornado affected Jackson County and another EF0 was observed in Jasper County.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The affected areas include near Marcelline, Jackson County, and Jasper County.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EF2 rating along with subsequent EF0 events indicate tornado activity.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind is the destructive hazard in these tornadoes.

Event_Names: 2023 Tornado in Hancock County and near Pawnee
Time_Annotation: August 6, 2023– A multi-vortex EFU tornado moved 8 miles through Hancock County, causing no damage, while a strong EF2 tornado damaged several homes north of Pawnee.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event mentions Hancock County and an area north of Pawnee.
Main_Event_Annotation: The EFU and EF2 designations indicate tornado events.
Hazards_Annotation: Wind damage is the associated hazard with these tornadoes.
